title: FDA-authorized AI devices
hook: The FDA has authorized a long and growing list of AI medical devices. This interactive registry lets anyone explore that list, and shows what it never records: whether a device was shown to help patients.
question: What does the FDA's public list of AI-enabled medical devices tell us, and what evidence about patient benefit is missing from it?
why_it_matters: Hospitals, clinicians, and patients may assume that an FDA-authorized AI device has been proven to work in patient care. Most of these devices reach the market by showing they resemble a device already sold, which does not require a new clinical trial. The official list records who made a device and when it was cleared, but not the clinical evidence behind it.
what_i_did: Downloaded the FDA's official list of AI-enabled medical devices and built a single self-contained web page around it.
Added search and filters by device, company, specialty, clearance pathway, and year, with charts that update as you filter.
Linked each submission number to its record in the FDA database.
Summarized published peer-reviewed studies of this list to show, in aggregate, what the authorization summaries report about clinical validation, with each figure cited to its source.
what_i_found: Nearly all devices on the list reached the market through the 510(k) pathway, which asks about similarity to an existing device rather than new clinical evidence.
Published reviews of the authorization summaries report that prospective real-world studies, demographic details of validation populations, and linked peer-reviewed publications are rare.
limits: The evidence summary comes from other researchers' published studies of the list as a whole, not from per-device review.
A snapshot of the FDA list at one download date; it does not update automatically.
